q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Find the highest-priority group first. Between an aldehyde and a ketone, which one becomes the suffix, and which carbon must then be C1?
w: An aldehyde outranks a ketone, so the parent is a pentanal and the CHO carbon is C1. Counting from the CHO carbon, the ketone C=O is at C4 and is named as the prefix oxo: 4-oxopentanal.
x: This gives the ketone the suffix, but an aldehyde has higher priority than a ketone, so the suffix must be -al.
The aldehyde carbon is C1, so the ketone sits at C4, not C2. 2-Oxopentanal is a different compound (a 1,2-dicarbonyl).
A CHO is named as a 'formyl' prefix only when the aldehyde is not the principal group; here it is the principal group, and the chain also includes the CHO carbon.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Ketone vs. alcohol: which group earns the suffix? Then number to give that group the lowest locant.
w: A ketone outranks an alcohol, so the suffix is -one and the OH becomes the prefix hydroxy. Numbering so the C=O gets the lowest number puts it at C2 and the OH at C4: 4-hydroxypentan-2-one.
x: The principal group (the ketone) must get the lowest possible locant; numbering from the other end gives it 4 instead of 2.
An alcohol ranks below a ketone, so -ol cannot be the suffix while a ketone is present.
The compound has no aldehyde (no H on the carbonyl carbon), and an internal carbon cannot carry -al.

q: What is the complete name of the compound shown, including its configuration?
h: The carbonyl carbon is C1; go around the ring in the direction that reaches the methyl soonest. For CIP, compare the two ring branches atom by atom until they differ.
w: The ring carbonyl carbon is C1 and numbering toward the methyl gives it locant 3 (not 5). At C3 the priorities are: CH2 toward C=O (C2, whose next atom is the carbonyl C bearing O,O,C) > CH2 on the other side (C4) > CH3 > H. With the lowest-priority H pointing away from the viewer, 1 → 2 → 3 runs clockwise: (R)-3-methylcyclohexan-1-one.
x: This reverses the configuration: with the C2 branch ranked over C4 and the H in back, the path turns clockwise, which is R.
Numbering the other way gives locant 5 instead of 3; lowest locants are required.
Both the locant (5 instead of 3) and the descriptor are wrong.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: When a CHO group is attached to a ring, the ring cannot absorb the aldehyde carbon into its name. What suffix is used then?
w: The aldehyde is the principal group. Because the CHO carbon is outside the ring, the suffix is -carbaldehyde and the ring carbon bearing it is C1. The ring ketone is a prefix, oxo, at C4: 4-oxocyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde.
x: This makes the ketone the principal group, but an aldehyde outranks a ketone.
The -al suffix is used only when the CHO carbon is part of the parent chain; a CHO on a ring needs -carbaldehyde.
The ketone is not the principal group, and the locants are inverted as well.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The ketone gets the lowest locant, ahead of the C=C. Then compare the higher-priority group on each alkene carbon.
w: The ketone is the principal group, so C1 is the methyl and the C=O is C2; the C=C is C3–C4 with the phenyl on C4. On C3 the higher-priority group is the acyl carbon; on C4 it is the phenyl. They are on opposite sides: (E)-4-phenylbut-3-en-2-one.
x: The acyl group and the phenyl lie on opposite sides of the C=C, which is E, not Z.
Numbering must give the principal group (the ketone) the lowest locant, so the ketone is at 2, not 3.
There is no aldehyde: the carbonyl carbon carries a methyl, not an H.

q: Rank these carbonyl compounds from most to least reactive toward nucleophilic addition.
h: Two effects: alkyl groups donate electron density to the carbonyl carbon, and they crowd the tetrahedral product. Count and size the groups.
w: Each alkyl group lowers the partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon (donation) and raises steric strain in the sp3 addition product. Formaldehyde (two H) is most reactive, then acetaldehyde (one alkyl), then acetone (two methyls), and pinacolone (methyl + bulky tert-butyl) is least: I > III > II > IV.
x: Formaldehyde has no alkyl groups at all, so it is more electrophilic and less hindered than acetaldehyde.
Acetone has two alkyl groups and acetaldehyde only one, so aldehydes rank above ketones.
A tert-butyl group crowds the tetrahedral product far more than a methyl, so pinacolone is less reactive than acetone, not more.

q: Which compound has the largest equilibrium constant for hydrate (gem-diol) formation in water?
h: What does an electron-withdrawing group next to the C=O do to the stability of the carbonyl compared with the hydrate?
w: Three chlorines pull electron density from the carbonyl carbon by induction, destabilizing the C=O and favoring the sp3 hydrate. Chloral (Cl3CCHO) exists almost entirely as the stable hydrate in water.
x: Acetaldehyde is roughly half hydrated in water, far less than chloral, because a methyl donates rather than withdraws electrons.
Acetone is a ketone with two donating methyls; its hydrate is only a tiny fraction at equilibrium.
Benzaldehyde's C=O is stabilized by conjugation with the ring, which disfavors hydrate formation.

q: Rank these compounds from largest to smallest equilibrium constant for cyanohydrin formation with HCN.
h: Addition destroys the conjugation between the C=O and the ring. Which para substituent makes the carbonyl carbon most electron-poor, and which donates into it? Where do ketones fall?
w: A para-nitro group withdraws electron density by resonance and induction, raising the carbonyl's electrophilicity (I largest). A para-methoxy group donates by resonance, stabilizing the C=O and lowering K (III below II). Acetophenone is a ketone: an extra methyl donates and crowds the adduct, so its K is far smaller than any of the aldehydes: I > II > III > IV.
x: This reverses the substituent effects: OCH<sub>3</sub> donates electron density into the C=O, making it less electrophilic, while NO<sub>2</sub> withdraws.
Even a donor-substituted benzaldehyde has a much larger K than a ketone; the extra alkyl group of acetophenone lowers K sharply.
An electron-withdrawing nitro group increases, not decreases, K relative to benzaldehyde.

q:
Consider these statements about the hydration of chloral, Cl3CCHO.
I. The CCl3 group withdraws electron density inductively and destabilizes the C=O.
II. In water, chloral lies mostly on the hydrate side, whereas acetone lies mostly on the carbonyl side.
III. The CCl3 group donates electrons to the carbonyl carbon by resonance, which stabilizes the hydrate.
Which statements are correct?
h: Can an sp<sup>3</sup> CCl<sub>3</sub> carbon take part in resonance with the C=O at all?
w: Statement I is the reason chloral hydrates so well: the inductive pull of three Cl atoms makes the C=O less stable relative to the gem-diol. Statement II is a true comparison (chloral is almost fully hydrated; acetone is <0.2% hydrated). Statement III is false: the sp3 CCl3 carbon has no π system to donate through, and donation would stabilize the carbonyl, not the hydrate. I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true: chloral is essentially all hydrate in water, while acetone is almost all ketone.
Statement III is false; CCl<sub>3</sub> acts only inductively (withdrawing), and it is not a resonance donor.
Statement III is false, so not all three can be correct.

q: Acetone is dissolved in H<sub>2</sub><sup>18</sup>O with a trace of acid. After some time, the acetone is recovered. Where is the <sup>18</sup>O label?
c: In the carbonyl oxygen of the recovered acetone
Nowhere; the hydrate equilibrium lies so far toward acetone that no exchange occurs
Only in the hydrate, which cannot lose water to re-form acetone
On the methyl carbons, by acid-catalyzed enolization
h: Hydrate formation is reversible. When the gem-diol loses water, which of its two OH groups can leave?
w: Even a small, fast hydrate equilibrium exchanges oxygen. Acetone + H218O ⇌ (CH3)2C(OH)(18OH); the gem-diol can lose either OH as water, so half the time it returns to acetone with 18O in the carbonyl. Repeated cycles enrich the label.
x: A small equilibrium constant does not stop exchange; the hydrate forms and reverts quickly, and that is all exchange requires.
Hydrate formation is reversible; the gem-diol readily loses water to re-form the C=O.
Enolization exchanges α-hydrogens, not oxygen; oxygen never moves onto a carbon.

q: Cyanohydrins are usually made from an aldehyde with NaCN (or KCN) and a controlled amount of acid, rather than with pure HCN. Why?
c: HCN is a weak acid, so free CN<sup>−</sup> (the real nucleophile) is needed; the acid then protonates the alkoxide
Pure HCN protonates the carbonyl oxygen so strongly that the aldehyde polymerizes instead of adding cyanide
CN<sup>−</sup> is a poor nucleophile, so the acid must first convert it into the more nucleophilic HCN
Acid is needed afterward to dehydrate the cyanohydrin to an α,β-unsaturated nitrile
h: Which species actually attacks the carbonyl carbon, and how much of it is present in pure HCN (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 9)?
w: The nucleophile is cyanide ion, and HCN (pKa ≈ 9.2) is barely ionized on its own, so the reaction with pure HCN is very slow. Supplying CN− from NaCN gives a good nucleophile; the alkoxide formed then takes a proton from HCN or the added acid, regenerating CN−. CN− is the nucleophile, and acid protonates the alkoxide.
x: HCN is too weak an acid to protonate a carbonyl significantly; the problem is the lack of cyanide ion, not polymerization.
This is backwards: the anion CN<sup>−</sup> is the nucleophile, while neutral HCN is a far weaker one.
Cyanohydrins are the desired products and are not dehydrated under these mild conditions.

q: Butan-2-one is treated with NaCN and HCl (aq). Which statement best describes the product?
c: Only (R)-2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanenitrile, because CN− attacks from the less hindered face
An achiral cyanohydrin, because the carbonyl carbon carries two alkyl groups
A meso cyanohydrin with two stereocenters
h: Is the new sp<sup>3</sup> carbon a stereocenter? Are the two faces of the planar C=O in butan-2-one different in any way that a cyanide ion could detect?
w: Addition creates C2 bearing OH, CN, CH3 and CH2CH3: a new stereocenter. The two faces of the planar C=O are enantiotopic, so with an achiral nucleophile and no chiral catalyst each face is attacked equally: a racemic mixture of 2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanenitrile.
x: Methyl and ethyl do not make one face of the C=O more hindered in a way an achiral reagent can tell apart; the faces are mirror images, so both enantiomers form equally.
The new carbon carries four different groups (OH, CN, CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>), so it is a stereocenter and the product is chiral.
Only one stereocenter forms, so a meso compound is impossible.

q: What is the final product of this sequence?
h: Step 1 adds CN and OH to the same carbon. What does LiAlH<sub>4</sub> do to a nitrile, and does it touch an alcohol?
w: Step 1 forms the cyanohydrin 1-hydroxycyclohexane-1-carbonitrile. LiAlH4 reduces the C≡N to CH2NH2 and leaves the tertiary OH in place: 1-(aminomethyl)cyclohexan-1-ol, a β-amino alcohol.
x: This is the product of nitrile hydrolysis (H3O+, heat), not reduction with LiAlH4.
The OH and CN were both on the ring carbon; reduction converts CN into CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, so the NH<sub>2</sub> ends up one carbon away, with the OH still on the ring.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> does not remove a tertiary OH; the alcohol survives.

q: Which species is an intermediate in the base-catalyzed (OH−) hydration of acetone?
h: Under base, the strong nucleophile attacks first. What does hydroxide add to, and what is formed directly?
w: In base, hydroxide attacks the neutral carbonyl carbon directly, giving the tetrahedral alkoxide (CH3)2C(OH)O−, which is then protonated by water to give the hydrate and regenerate OH−.
x: The protonated carbonyl is the activated electrophile in the acid-catalyzed path; there is no strong acid in basic solution.
A protonated gem-diol (oxonium) is an acid-catalyzed intermediate, not one formed in hydroxide solution.
The enol forms by tautomerization, a different process; it is not on the path to the hydrate.

q: Cyclohexanone gives a high yield of cyanohydrin with HCN/CN<sup>−</sup>, but 2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexanone gives almost none. What is the best explanation?
c: The three α-methyl groups crowd the tetrahedral adduct, so the reversible equilibrium favors the ketone
The methyl groups make the ketone so acidic that CN<sup>−</sup> deprotonates it at the α-carbon instead of adding to C=O
The trimethyl ketone has no α-hydrogens left, so it cannot form a cyanohydrin by any path
The methyl groups withdraw electron density, making the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic
h: Cyanohydrin formation is reversible. What happens to steric strain when the carbonyl carbon goes from sp<sup>2</sup> (120°) to sp<sup>3</sup> (109.5°)?
w: Cyanohydrin formation is an equilibrium. On going from sp2 to sp3, the new OH and CN groups are pressed against the three neighboring α-methyl groups; that strain makes the adduct much less stable, so the equilibrium lies toward the hindered ketone.
x: α-Methyl groups do not make the ketone notably more acidic, and cyanide is too weak a base to enolize it significantly.
C6 still bears one α-hydrogen, and cyanohydrin formation does not need α-hydrogens anyway (benzaldehyde has none).
Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating; their electronic effect is small here compared with the steric strain.
